title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–2)
hook: after Tisha B'Av, prophetic readings of comfort begin

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wolf and the lamb lay down together, and a little child leads them. Did an unlikely pair make peace anywhere near you? Today, Isaiah turns a page and changes his voice. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

Chapter thirty-nine of Isaiah holds a warning: the treasures of the king's house will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then chapter forty opens with a different sound entirely. Not a warning. Not a reason. Two words, the same word twice: Nachamu, nachamu. Comfort, comfort. There is a Shabbat in the Jewish year named after that word. It comes right after Tisha B'Av, the fast of mourning for the fallen Temple, and synagogues read these verses on it. A day of grief, and then, the very next Shabbat, comfort.
screen: `A WARNING ABOUT BABYLON.` → `THEN: NACHAMU, NACHAMU.` → `THE SHABBAT AFTER TISHA B'AV.`

segments.voice: Here is how the chapter begins, in the King James words: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Notice the ye. The command is plural. God isn't comforting the people directly here; God is telling a group, unnamed, to go and do it. Some readers hear prophets, some hear angels, some hear anyone within earshot. Comfort, in this verse, is a job handed out. And the word is doubled. Comfort, comfort. Once wasn't enough. Then the next line: "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem." The Hebrew is warmer than the English. It says, literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. Not at her. Not about her. To her heart. And what are the comforters told to say? That her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received double for all her sins. This comfort doesn't pretend nothing happened. It names the war. It names the wrong. It just says: it is over now. That shape lives on in an ordinary Jewish custom. When people visit a house of mourning, there is a traditional sentence said to the mourners as they leave, asking that God comfort them among the other mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. Same word for comfort. Same city. The private loss in one living room is set beside the old loss of a whole people, and both are spoken to the heart. Comfort, in this chapter, is less a feeling than a visit.
screen: `THE COMMAND IS PLURAL.` · `COMFORT, COMFORT: SAID TWICE.` · `SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.` · `IT NAMES THE LOSS, THEN SAYS: IT IS OVER.` · then, large: `COMFORT YE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort one person. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind who is carrying something heavy right now: a loss, a diagnosis, a long hard season. Don't solve it. Just ask what speaking to their heart would sound like. Not advice. Not a reason. Maybe just: I'm thinking of you. I'm here. Decide how you'll say it today, a call, a note, a visit. If you pray, you can hold the verse's two words for them: comfort, comfort. The bell holds the time.
Nachamu. Comfort ye, a plural command, said twice at the start of Isaiah forty, and the name of the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av. Today's word.
Your line: comfort ye my people. Today, send the message you decided on, and speak to the heart, not at it. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Isaiah 40 is read in synagogue on Shabbat Nachamu, the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, and Jews visiting a house of mourning traditionally offer a set line of comfort that names the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem.

myth: in Isaiah 40, God comforts the people directly
God tells a group to do it: comfort ye. the comfort is a job handed out.
the comfort pretends nothing was lost
it names the war and the wrong, then says it is over.
a Shabbat is named after this verse's first word
Shabbat Nachamu, right after Tisha B'Av.

fork.setup: you're the prophet. the warnings came true, and the people are grieving. what is your first word to them?
options: a long explanation of why it happened.
fork.reveal: "comfort ye, comfort ye my people." the chapter after a warning opens with the same word twice.

original.note: Hebrew: comfort, comfort my people, the opening of Isaiah 40.

trapdoor: what you thought: God saying something gentle.
what it means: God sends others to comfort a grieving city, and to speak to her heart.
what a scholar hears: nachamu is a plural command, doubled, and dabru al lev, speak to the heart, is the Hebrew behind speak ye comfortably.

sources.quoted: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): hook verb 'carries ... carried off' smoothed; myth 1 reworded (it said 'God is told to comfort', which garbled the point). Path-wide: Judaism path quotes KJV, not JPS 1917 as SCRIPT_GUIDE asks; Keeper to decide.
Editor: hook no longer says chapter 39 'closes' with the warning (it ends on Hezekiah's reply) and drops 'the scroll goes quiet', an implied manuscript claim; varied one 'notice' line.
Index hook says 'seven prophetic readings of comfort'; the count was dropped under the claims rule (no cited text gives it). Keeper may restore the seven haftarot of consolation if wanted.
Shabbat Nachamu as the Shabbat after Tisha B'Av, with Isaiah 40 as its haftarah: confirm phrasing 'synagogues read these verses on it'.
'Speak to the heart of Jerusalem' as the literal Hebrew (dabru al lev) of 40:2: confirm.
Who the plural 'ye' addresses: the script offers prophets, angels or anyone, without ranking (Targum and commentators differ). Confirm.
The mourners' formula (HaMakom yenachem etchem...) is described, not quoted; confirm the description and that it shares the root of nachamu.
KJV quoted because I was not certain of the exact JPS 1917 wording.
